questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I am interested in Arctic studies and I was excited to live and study in a different part of the Arctic (prior to my MSc I lived in Alaska). Nuuk also offered the opportunity to be involved in scientific research in the Arctic alongside my academic studies.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy. -NAME REDACTED-, the international student coordinator at Ilisimatusarfik, is extremely helpful. He gave me a tour of campus on my first day, introduced me to other students and was available to answer any questions I had during the term.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Because I organized a project outside course scope at Greenland Institute of Natural Resources, GINR allowed me to stay in one of their housing buildings, which was affordable and conveniently located on the same campus as both the Institute and the university.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I think most people found it relatively difficult to find off campus housing, because it is organized through the local housing authority. I lucked out because I worked with the Institute and could stay in their housing.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I'm really not the best person to ask, as I didn't really have to search for housing, it just fell into my lap.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was limited in the number of courses taught in English at Ilisimatusarfik (only two at the master's level during fall 2025). Ultimately this ended up being a good thing because it forced me to find a research project to make up the last 10 ECTS of my semester and I ended up really enjoying working at Greenland Institute of Natural Resources.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Just had to email the international student coordinator my choices, and he registered me.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: -NAME REDACTED- was very helpful, although it wasn't super clear what the courses were about before I was registered. The course catalog gave only a cursory description, not a full syllabus.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Successful, but see above.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Ilisimatusarfik is a small school, so you might not have a lot of course options, especially if you don't speak Danish or Greenlandic. Still, the experience of being in Nuuk is way bigger than just your course choices so I would not weigh that too heavily in your decision to study in Greenland.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Both courses felt appropriate for my level.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I'm used to more group project based learning at KU and we didn't really do project work in my Ilisimatusarfik courses. Courses were mostly lecture-based with individual projects at the end.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Arctic Economy
Advanced Economic Methodology

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Arctic Economy was really interesting, especially if you are interested in learning about how the Arctic economic development, natural resources and social issues.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Flights to and from Greenland are incredibly expensive. Food is more expensive than in Copenhagen but less than I thought it would be.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The university does a good job making sure the international students have opportunities to socialize. They organized a fishing trip for us at the start of the semester and a biweekly (every other week) kaffemik to have coffee, cake and socialize. We did not have a lot of opportunities to mix with local students but I think that has more to do with the culture of the university. Many students are also parents or have jobs in addition to their studies, so they don't stay on campus beyond class time for the most part.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Most of my time was taken up by school, research and a part time job, so I didn't look into student organizations much, but I did spend a fair amount of time with my fellow international students.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Rock climbing at the børnehave, volunteer at the animal shelter, go to the pub quiz at Daddy's on Thursday nights, attend cultural events at Katuaq, go hiking or look for northern lights, take a boat tour into the fjords or (more expensive) take the ferry to Ilulissat for a few days.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Reasonably easy. Nuuk is a bustling city and most people speak Danish. To me the culture shared similarities with both Alaska and Denmark, in terms of the language and traditions, so I didn't feel like it was hard to adjust. Certainly you're still an outsider, so I think it's best to be open, observe and ask (respectful) questions.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I could have done a better job at making stronger connections with local students but I did make a point to ask other students questions during class breaks and say hi when I saw people around town. Even though most local students have their own busy lives I found everyone to be friendly and welcoming.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not speaking Greenlandic definitely limits the level of communication and integrating you can do, but most people also speak Danish and many speak English as well.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I found people very friendly and welcoming and curious about me, so even though I was new and an outsider, I felt a lot of warmth. There are also a lot of cultural events, arts, music and theater, happening in Nuuk so it was easy to attend and learn more about Greenland's culture.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Book flights early before prices go up.
2. Find housing early, try to look at bus routes when you choose where to live.
3. Academics are only a small part of your time in Greenland, try to experience as much as you can while you're there, get outside and out of the city if possible.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: n/a

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting to experience the incredible nature of Greenland with new friends who are also interested in the Arctic.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I was pretty homesick for the first couple months, as it took me awhile to feel comfortable in my new community, even with a lot of new people around to be friends with.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
